title: Light poured out
hookLine: sunlight seems poured down but is never used up (Meditations 8.57)

lines: A PATCH OF LIGHT ON THE FLOOR.
cards: Sit in a room with one window on a sunny afternoon and watch the patch of light on the floor. It's been pouring in all day, more every minute, and the window never runs dry. The sun never sends a bill.
Nobody has to refill it. In book eight of his Meditations, Marcus noticed the same plain thing, sunlight coming in, and found in it a picture of how a mind should move through the world.

teach.b: The sun's light seems poured down, Marcus says, spread out in every direction, and yet it isn't poured away. It isn't used up. The spreading is a kind of stretching out.
The Greek word for rays is aktines, and Marcus says they're called that from a verb meaning to be stretched out.
It's his own word play; the point isn't the dictionary but the picture: light reaches out without leaving its source. Next, watch sunlight come through a narrow opening into a dark house.

teach.h: THE BEAM RESTS ON WHAT IT MEETS.
teach.b: It travels in a straight line, and when it meets something solid that blocks it, it rests there. It doesn't slide off or fall. It just lights up what's in front of it.

teach.h: A MIND THAT POURS, NOT CRASHES.
teach.b: That's how Marcus wants his own mind to pour itself out: not emptied, not crashing violently into whatever stands in the way, but resting on it, lighting whatever will take the light.
And if something refuses it, he says, that thing only deprives itself.
So attention, warmth, effort, given like sunlight, can reach far and still not run out, as long as they're poured, not thrown.

how: Some readers of Marcus use sunlight as a daily reminder: a few minutes in the light, and then attention given to others the way it falls, steady and unforced.

games.q: you're the beam of light coming into a dark room, and you hit a wall. what do you do?
o: crash against it until it gives.
slide off and go somewhere else.
rest on it, and light up what's there.
games.why: Marcus says the light stays fixed where it meets a solid body, neither glancing off nor falling, and lights what receives it.

practice: If you can, move into sunlight, a window or a patch on the floor; if it's night, picture one. Let it rest on your hands, and notice that it doesn't push or rush; it just arrives and stays.
Then think of one person you'll see today, and imagine your attention reaching them like that, steady and warm, not forcing, not running out.

wordCard.voice: Aktines. Marcus's Greek word for the sun's rays: stretched out in every direction, never used up, resting on what they meet. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a ray of light (plural aktines). Marcus links it, playfully, to a verb meaning to stretch out.
